profile.name: Classical Ballet
profile.tagline: A formal, rigorous theatrical dance tradition rooted in 17th-century French courts.
profile.insight: In 1661, King Louis XIV established the Académie Royale de Danse to formalize ballet, transforming it from an aristocratic amateur pastime into a professional discipline defined by turnout and precision.
profile.profile: Classical ballet is a formal, theatrical dance style characterized by rigorous technique, including turnout, pointe work, and high extensions. Originating in Italian Renaissance courts and refined in 17th-century France, it relies on a standardized vocabulary of movements and positions. Today, it is practiced globally through various training systems that emphasize strength, flexibility, and precise body alignment.
profile.profile_long:
Classical ballet stands as one of the most formal and technically demanding theatrical dance traditions in the world. Its origins trace back to the Italian Renaissance courts, where dance served as a social and ceremonial activity for the aristocracy. In the 16th century, Catherine de' Medici brought these courtly traditions to France, where they began to evolve. Initially, these performances were executed by aristocratic amateurs, but as the 17th century progressed, ballet shifted toward a professional art form. King Louis XIV, a central figure in this transition, established the Académie Royale de Danse in 1661 to improve training standards and codify the discipline. Under the guidance of dancing-master Pierre Beauchamp, the five fundamental positions of the feet—which remain the bedrock of classical ballet today—were established. 

The development of classical ballet continued through the Romantic era, characterized by storytelling and a softer aesthetic, eventually culminating in the classical era. This shift was largely driven by Marius Petipa, a choreographer who integrated the narrative elements of Romantic ballet with the athletic rigor of Russian technique. Petipa’s influence cemented structural elements such as the grand pas de deux and the standardized use of the corps de ballet. 

Technique in classical ballet is defined by specific principles, most notably 'turnout,' the outward rotation of the legs and feet originating from the hip. This technique, originally popularized by Louis XIV, allows for greater range of motion and aesthetic line. Dancers strive for 'ballon,' the appearance of floating during jumps, and utilize 'spotting' to maintain balance during turns. Advanced dancers, typically after years of training and once their feet have fully developed, may progress to pointe work, where the body’s weight is supported on the tips of the toes in specially designed shoes. 

Training is highly structured, with students learning terminology in French and focusing on core strength, flexibility, and precise body form. Various training systems exist globally, each producing a unique aesthetic. These include the Vaganova and Legat methods from Russia, the Cecchetti method from Italy, the Bournonville method from Denmark, and the Royal Academy of Dance (RAD) method. While some schools follow these standardized systems, others, such as the American-style Balanchine method or various French schools, employ unique approaches. 

Music has played a vital role in the evolution of the classroom. In the 18th century, ballet masters played the violin to guide students through exercises. By the 20th century, the piano became the standard accompaniment. The relationship between the teacher and the musician is considered essential, as the musician often improvises to support the specific needs of the dancers. 

Attire is designed to reveal the body’s lines, allowing teachers to evaluate alignment. Female dancers typically wear leotards, tights, and soft shoes, transitioning to pointe shoes as they advance. Male dancers wear tights and form-fitting shirts, often utilizing a dance belt for support. The tradition remains a living art form, continuously taught and performed in companies and schools worldwide, maintaining a consistent vocabulary while allowing for regional stylistic variations.

sections.origins_and_history: Classical ballet originated in Italian Renaissance courts, moving to France in the 16th century. King Louis XIV founded the Académie Royale de Danse in 1661, and Pierre Beauchamp codified the five positions of the feet. The classical era was later defined by Marius Petipa, who combined Romantic storytelling with Russian athletic technique.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers utilize turnout, five positions of the feet, and precise arm movements. Technique includes jumps (ballon), turns using spotting, and pointe work for advanced female dancers. Training emphasizes core strength and flexibility.
sections.music_and_instruments: Historically accompanied by a violin played by the teacher. In modern times, the piano is the standard instrument for class, with musicians often improvising to match the tempo and mood of the exercises.
sections.costume_and_setting: Female dancers wear leotards, tights, and soft shoes (or pointe shoes). Male dancers wear tights and fitted shirts. Settings include dance studios with mirrors and stages for performance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ballet is a theatrical art form performed for audiences. It serves as a discipline for professional dancers and a rigorous physical practice for students.
sections.notable_figures: Marius Petipa, Anna Pavlova, Margot Fonteyn, Rudolf Nureyev, Enrico Cecchetti, Agrippina Vaganova, Nikolai Legat, August Bournonville.
sections.regional_variants: Russian ballet (high extensions, dynamic turns), Italian ballet (grounded, intricate footwork), French ballet, and British ballet.
sections.lineage: Evolved from Renaissance court dances, through the Romantic era, into the classical era defined by Petipa.

teaching.level_notes: Training is divided into levels based on strength, flexibility, and technical proficiency.

music_profile.sound_description: Music for ballet class is typically played on piano, with the musician improvising or selecting repertoire to match the specific rhythm and energy of the teacher's exercises.

movement_profile.posture: Upright, aligned, with turnout emanating from the hips.
movement_profile.footwork: Based on five fundamental positions of the feet, performed with turnout.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Five positions of the arms, standardized to complement the feet.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Strong core engagement; turnout originates from the hip joint.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Standardized layouts for stage and studio reference points.
movement_profile.partnering: Includes lifts and support, typically introduced as dancers gain strength.

signature_moves.name: Pointe work
signature_moves.description: Supporting body weight on the tips of fully extended feet in pointe shoes.

signature_moves.name: Turnout
signature_moves.description: Outward rotation of the legs and feet from the hip.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Includes jumps (ballon) and turns using spotting.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Premature pointe work before feet are fully developed (typically before age 12).

episode_brief.logline: Discover the rigorous history and precise technique that transformed courtly dance into the global art of classical ballet.
